_meta.description: PatientTriage.ai Clinical Knowledge Base — illustrative/synthetic data for prototype only. Not clinically validated.

domains.label: Cardiac / ACS
domains.complexity_rationale: Potential Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) or arrhythmia. Risk of rapid hemodynamic compromise requiring immediate intervention.
monitoring_criteria: 12-Lead ECG changes (ST elevation, ST depression, T-wave inversions, new LBBB)
Serial cardiac troponin I/T levels (elevation indicates myocardial necrosis)
Pain radiation pattern to jaw, neck, or left arm
Hemodynamic stability: BP, HR, skin perfusion
Rhythm monitoring for arrhythmias
preliminary_tests: 12-Lead ECG (within 10 minutes of arrival — STEMI alert if indicated)
Serial Cardiac Troponins I or T (0h/2h/6h protocol)
Chest X-Ray (CXR) — exclude aortic dissection, pneumothorax, pulmonary oedema
Point-of-care BNP or NT-proBNP if heart failure suspected

emergency_medications.name: Aspirin (Chewable)
emergency_medications.dosage: 300 mg PO (chewed, not swallowed whole)
emergency_medications.indication: Suspected ACS / STEMI / NSTEMI
emergency_medications.warning: Contraindicated with active GI bleed, severe bleeding disorders, or documented aspirin allergy. Do not give if aortic dissection is suspected.

emergency_medications.name: Nitroglycerin (Sublingual)
emergency_medications.dosage: 0.4 mg SL q5min (max 3 doses)
emergency_medications.indication: Active anginal chest pain
emergency_medications.warning: Hold if systolic BP <90 mmHg, HR <50 or >100, or patient used PDE-5 inhibitor (sildenafil/tadalafil) within 24–48h. Can precipitate hypotension.

emergency_medications.name: Morphine Sulfate (IV)
emergency_medications.dosage: 2–4 mg IV q5–15 min titrated to pain
emergency_medications.indication: Refractory chest pain in confirmed ACS only
emergency_medications.warning: Use with caution — may mask symptoms. Avoid if hypotensive or respiratory compromise. Evidence suggests possible harm in NSTEMI.

age_modifiers.geriatric: Atypical presentations common (fatigue, dyspnea, syncope without classic chest pain). Lower threshold for ACS workup. Higher bleeding risk with anticoagulation.
age_modifiers.pediatric: ACS rare in children. Consider myocarditis, pericarditis, or congenital cardiac anomaly. Kawasaki disease in <5y with fever.
age_modifiers.adult: Classic presentation more common. HEART score calculation recommended.

domains.label: Respiratory / Airway
domains.complexity_rationale: Acute respiratory compromise. Risk of hypoxic respiratory failure, respiratory arrest, or airway occlusion without prompt intervention.
monitoring_criteria: SpO2 continuously (target >94%; COPD target 88–92%)
Work of breathing: accessory muscle use, intercostal retractions, nasal flaring
Respiratory rate and breath sounds (wheeze, crackles, silent chest, stridor)
Mental status changes (hypoxia and hypercapnia can both cause confusion)
Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) in asthma
preliminary_tests: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) if severe distress or SpO2 <92%

emergency_medications.name: Salbutamol/Albuterol (Nebulised)
emergency_medications.dosage: 2.5–5 mg nebulised q20min for 3 doses, then q1–4h
emergency_medications.indication: Bronchospasm, acute asthma, COPD exacerbation
emergency_medications.warning: Monitor HR — can cause tachycardia, tremor, hypokalaemia. Use with caution in ischaemic heart disease.

emergency_medications.name: Ipratropium Bromide (Nebulised)
emergency_medications.dosage: 0.5 mg nebulised q20min for 3 doses
emergency_medications.indication: COPD exacerbation, moderate–severe asthma
emergency_medications.warning: Can cause urinary retention in elderly males. Avoid eye contact.

emergency_medications.name: Methylprednisolone (IV) / Prednisolone (PO)
emergency_medications.dosage: IV: 40–125 mg; PO: 40–50 mg once daily for 5 days
emergency_medications.indication: Systemic corticosteroid for asthma/COPD flare
emergency_medications.warning: Monitor blood glucose especially in diabetics. Not a bronchodilator — does not provide immediate relief.

age_modifiers.geriatric: Reduced respiratory reserve. Silent chest may indicate near-fatal asthma. COPD exacerbations often triggered by infection. Watch for ventilatory fatigue.
age_modifiers.pediatric: Asthma most common. Use weight-based dosing. Stridor suggests croup or epiglottitis — do not agitate child. Bronchiolitis (RSV) in <2y.
age_modifiers.adult: Standard presentation. Assess CURB-65 if pneumonia suspected.

domains.label: Neurological / Stroke / Seizure
domains.complexity_rationale: Time-critical neurological emergency. Brain tissue loss in ischaemic stroke: ~1.9 million neurons per minute without reperfusion.
monitoring_criteria: FAST: Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time of onset
Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) or AVPU — document and trend
Pupillary response: size, symmetry, reactivity
Blood glucose: hypoglycaemia mimics stroke
BP monitoring: permissive hypertension in acute ischaemic stroke unless >185/110 (thrombolysis threshold)
preliminary_tests: Non-contrast CT Head (within 25 min of arrival — exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis)
MRI Brain + DWI if CT negative but stroke strongly suspected
EEG if subclinical seizure activity suspected

emergency_medications.name: Alteplase (tPA)
emergency_medications.dosage: 0.9 mg/kg IV (max 90 mg); 10% bolus over 1 min, remainder over 60 min
emergency_medications.indication: Acute ischaemic stroke, onset <4.5h, haemorrhage excluded on CT
emergency_medications.warning: CRITICAL: Must exclude haemorrhage first. Absolute contraindications: active bleeding, recent surgery, platelet <100k, recent anticoagulant use. Activate stroke team.

emergency_medications.name: Levetiracetam (IV)
emergency_medications.dosage: 500–1500 mg IV loading dose over 15 min
emergency_medications.indication: Active or recurring seizures
emergency_medications.warning: Infuse slowly. Monitor for somnolence, agitation, or behavioural changes. Reduce dose in renal impairment.

emergency_medications.name: Lorazepam (IV/IM)
emergency_medications.dosage: 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg per dose) — repeat once if needed
emergency_medications.indication: Status epilepticus or acute seizure termination
emergency_medications.warning: Causes respiratory depression — have airway equipment ready. Do not use if haemodynamically unstable without airway control.

age_modifiers.geriatric: Falls with head injury risk. Atrial fibrillation-related embolic stroke more common. Anticoagulant use affects thrombolysis eligibility.
age_modifiers.pediatric: Seizures common (febrile). True stroke rare — consider ADEM, venous sinus thrombosis. Weight-based anticonvulsant dosing mandatory.
age_modifiers.adult: Standard FAST assessment. NIHSS scoring recommended for stroke severity.

domains.label: Sepsis / Systemic Infection
domains.complexity_rationale: Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by dysregulated host response to infection. Mortality increases 7% per hour without antibiotics in septic shock.
monitoring_criteria: qSOFA: Respiratory rate ≥22, Altered mental status, Systolic BP ≤100
SOFA score organs: PaO2/FiO2, GCS, MAP, creatinine, bilirubin, platelets
Lactate trend (target <2 mmol/L with treatment)
Fluid responsiveness: MAP, HR, urine output (target ≥0.5 mL/kg/h)
Temperature trend and source identification
preliminary_tests: Blood Cultures ×2 sets from different sites (before antibiotics)
Serum Lactate (urgent — elevated >2 mmol/L indicates tissue hypoperfusion)
Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (renal and hepatic function)
Chest X-Ray if respiratory source suspected

emergency_medications.name: Piperacillin-Tazobactam (IV)
emergency_medications.dosage: 4.5 g IV q6–8h (adjust for renal function)
emergency_medications.indication: Broad-spectrum empirical coverage for sepsis of unknown source
emergency_medications.warning: Adjust dose in renal impairment. Check allergy (penicillin). Obtain cultures BEFORE starting antibiotics.

emergency_medications.name: Ceftriaxone (IV)
emergency_medications.dosage: 2 g IV q24h
emergency_medications.indication: Community-acquired sepsis, meningitis cover (add dexamethasone), urological sepsis
emergency_medications.warning: Verify cephalosporin/penicillin allergies. Avoid concurrent administration with calcium-containing IV fluids.

emergency_medications.name: Crystalloid Fluid Bolus (IV)
emergency_medications.dosage: 30 mL/kg IV over 3h (reassess after each 500 mL bolus)
emergency_medications.indication: Sepsis-induced hypotension or hypoperfusion
emergency_medications.warning: Reassess frequently. Excess fluid causes pulmonary oedema — use dynamic measures (stroke volume variation, pulse pressure variation) to guide resuscitation. Caution in CHF/ESRD.

age_modifiers.geriatric: Hypothermia or normal temperature possible despite severe sepsis. Atypical presentation: confusion, falls, functional decline. Higher mortality.
age_modifiers.pediatric: Paediatric SOFA differs. Age-specific vital sign thresholds critical. Meningococcal septicaemia: non-blanching rash — medical emergency.
age_modifiers.adult: Hour-1 bundle: culture, lactate, antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors if refractory.

domains.label: Allergic Reaction / Anaphylaxis
domains.complexity_rationale: Anaphylaxis is potentially fatal within minutes. Airway oedema, bronchospasm, and distributive shock can develop simultaneously.
monitoring_criteria: Airway patency: stridor, hoarseness, drooling (angioedema)
Haemodynamic status: hypotension indicates anaphylactic shock
Skin progression: urticaria spreading, angioedema extending to airway
SpO2 and respiratory effort
Response to epinephrine (should see improvement within 5–15 min)
preliminary_tests: Serum tryptase (draw within 1–3h of reaction for confirmation)

emergency_medications.name: Adrenaline/Epinephrine (IM)
emergency_medications.dosage: 0.5 mg (1:1000) IM into lateral thigh — child: 0.01 mg/kg
emergency_medications.indication: FIRST-LINE treatment for anaphylaxis. Any sign of airway involvement, bronchospasm, or hypotension.
emergency_medications.warning: Repeat every 5–15 min if symptoms persist or recur. If no IM response, consider 0.1 mg IV (1:10,000) titrated. Autoinjector (EpiPen) acceptable if IM unavailable.

emergency_medications.name: Chlorphenamine (IV/IM)
emergency_medications.dosage: 10 mg IV/IM slowly
emergency_medications.indication: Antihistamine — adjunct for urticaria and pruritus
emergency_medications.warning: NOT first-line for anaphylaxis. Does not treat airway oedema or shock. Can cause sedation and hypotension.

emergency_medications.name: Hydrocortisone (IV)
emergency_medications.dosage: 200 mg IV slowly
emergency_medications.indication: Prevent biphasic reaction — adjunct after adrenaline
emergency_medications.warning: Delayed onset (~4–6h). Do not substitute for adrenaline. Monitor blood glucose.

age_modifiers.geriatric: Beta-blockers may attenuate response to epinephrine — consider glucagon 1–2 mg IV/IM. Higher aspiration risk.
age_modifiers.pediatric: Weight-based adrenaline dosing (0.01 mg/kg IM, max 0.5 mg). EpiPen Jr for <30 kg. Avoid prone positioning.
age_modifiers.adult: Identify and remove trigger. Observe minimum 6h for biphasic reaction before discharge.

domains.label: Trauma / Orthopaedic / Bleeding
domains.complexity_rationale: Acute trauma requires rapid haemorrhage control, neurovascular assessment, and pain management. Occult internal bleeding risk in high-energy mechanisms.
monitoring_criteria: Haemorrhage control: rate of bleeding, response to direct pressure
Neurovascular status distal to injury: pulse, sensation, motor function, capillary refill
GCS trend in head injuries
Deformity, joint range of motion, weight-bearing capability
Haemodynamic stability: HR and BP trend with blood loss
preliminary_tests: Plain Radiography (X-Ray) of the affected extremity or spine
FAST ultrasound (focused assessment with sonography in trauma) if abdominal trauma
CT Head + C-Spine if head injury with LOC, amnesia, or GCS <15
Group & Screen / Crossmatch if transfusion risk

emergency_medications.name: Tranexamic Acid (TXA) (IV)
emergency_medications.dosage: 1 g IV over 10 min (must give within 3h of injury)
emergency_medications.indication: Significant haemorrhage or haemorrhage risk in major trauma
emergency_medications.warning: Not indicated after 3h — may increase mortality. Contraindicated in isolated head injury without systemic haemorrhage.

emergency_medications.name: Ketorolac (IV/IM)
emergency_medications.dosage: 15–30 mg IV/IM (adult, single dose)
emergency_medications.indication: Moderate-to-severe acute musculoskeletal pain
emergency_medications.warning: Contraindicated in renal impairment, active peptic ulcer, bleeding disorders, or suspected intracranial bleed. Max 5 days use.

age_modifiers.geriatric: Low-energy falls (e.g. from standing) can cause significant fractures (hip, vertebral) due to osteoporosis. Higher risk of occult intracranial injury. Anticoagulant use increases bleeding risk.
age_modifiers.pediatric: Non-accidental injury (NAI) must be considered if mechanism inconsistent with injury pattern or age. Greenstick fractures common. Epiphyseal injuries may not show on initial X-ray.
age_modifiers.adult: Mechanism guides investigation. High-energy mechanisms require systematic primary survey (ATLS).

domains.label: Abdominal / GI
domains.complexity_rationale: Broad differential including surgical emergencies (appendicitis, perforation, obstruction) and medical causes. Peritonitis carries high mortality if untreated.
monitoring_criteria: Abdominal tenderness: localised vs diffuse, rebound tenderness, guarding (peritonism)
Hydration status: mucous membranes, skin turgor, urine output, HR/BP
Bowel sounds
Ability to tolerate oral intake
Serial abdominal exams if diagnosis unclear
preliminary_tests: Abdominal Ultrasound (first-line for RUQ and appendix)
CT Abdomen/Pelvis with contrast (if US inconclusive or surgical emergency suspected)
Urinary hCG in females of childbearing age (ectopic exclusion)
Erect CXR if perforation suspected (free air under diaphragm)

emergency_medications.name: Ondansetron (IV/ODT)
emergency_medications.dosage: 4–8 mg IV slowly or 8 mg ODT
emergency_medications.indication: Severe nausea or active vomiting
emergency_medications.warning: Prolongs QT interval. Use with caution in patients at risk for arrhythmia or on other QT-prolonging agents.

emergency_medications.name: Morphine Sulfate (IV)
emergency_medications.dosage: 2.5–5 mg IV q4h PRN
emergency_medications.indication: Moderate-to-severe abdominal pain (adequate analgesia does not mask diagnosis)
emergency_medications.warning: Titrate to pain. Monitor respiratory rate and sedation. Caution in hepatic failure.

age_modifiers.geriatric: Atypical presentations common (e.g. appendicitis without classic signs). Higher perforation risk due to delayed presentation. Mesenteric ischaemia in AF patients.
age_modifiers.pediatric: Appendicitis peaks 10–12y. Intussusception in <3y (redcurrant jelly stool). Malrotation in neonates.
age_modifiers.adult: Ectopic pregnancy must be excluded in females of reproductive age. Renal colic common cause of flank/abdominal pain.

domains.label: Obstetric / Gynaecological
domains.complexity_rationale: Obstetric emergencies carry significant maternal and fetal mortality. Ectopic rupture and eclampsia can be immediately life-threatening.
monitoring_criteria: Gestational age and fetal monitoring (if viable gestational age)
Haemodynamic stability in suspected ectopic rupture
Blood pressure trend for pre-eclampsia (≥140/90 with proteinuria)
Seizure activity in eclampsia
Fetal heart rate (if ≥24 weeks)

emergency_medications.name: Magnesium Sulfate (IV)
emergency_medications.dosage: 4 g IV loading dose over 20 min, then 1 g/h maintenance
emergency_medications.indication: Eclampsia seizure prevention and treatment
emergency_medications.warning: Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output hourly. Antidote: calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% IV. Toxicity causes respiratory arrest.

age_modifiers.geriatric: Less applicable — consider uterine prolapse, gynaecological malignancy.
age_modifiers.pediatric: Adolescent ectopic possible. Consider NAI if pelvic injury without clear mechanism.
age_modifiers.adult: Standard obstetric protocols apply. Always involve obstetric team early.

domains.label: Psychiatric / Mental Health
domains.complexity_rationale: Risk of deliberate self-harm or harm to others. Medical stabilisation must precede psychiatric assessment. Overdose may have delayed toxicity.
monitoring_criteria: Safety risk assessment: suicidal ideation, plan, means, intent
Level of agitation and risk to staff
Toxidrome identification (pupil size, HR, BP, temperature, diaphoresis)
GCS if overdose or substance use
preliminary_tests: Paracetamol/acetaminophen level (even if not suspected — commonly taken in overdose)
ECG (QT prolongation in tricyclic antidepressant overdose)

emergency_medications.name: Naloxone (IM/IV/Intranasal)
emergency_medications.dosage: 0.4–2 mg IV/IM q2–3min; 4 mg intranasal
emergency_medications.indication: Opioid overdose (suspected decreased respiratory drive, pinpoint pupils, miosis)
emergency_medications.warning: Short half-life — may need infusion or repeated doses. Can precipitate acute withdrawal. Caution in opioid-dependent patients.

emergency_medications.name: N-Acetylcysteine (IV)
emergency_medications.dosage: 150 mg/kg over 15–60 min, then 50 mg/kg over 4h, then 100 mg/kg over 16h
emergency_medications.indication: Paracetamol/acetaminophen overdose — within 24h (most effective within 8h)
emergency_medications.warning: Can cause anaphylactoid reaction — slow infusion rate if occurs. Do not delay for symptom absence.

age_modifiers.geriatric: Drug interactions and polypharmacy. Overdose may be accidental. Cognitive impairment affects capacity assessment.
age_modifiers.pediatric: Careful history from carers. Consider NAI. Accidental ingestion most common in young children.
age_modifiers.adult: Risk-stratify for disposition. Medically clear before psychiatric review.

domains.label: Toxicology / Poisoning
domains.complexity_rationale: Toxicological emergencies have delayed presentation and variable time courses. Some agents (paracetamol, digoxin) have peak toxicity hours after ingestion.
monitoring_criteria: Toxidrome identification: cholinergic, sympathomimetic, opioid, anticholinergic, serotonin syndrome
Continuous cardiac monitoring (QRS widening, QT prolongation)
Mental status and GCS trend
Respiratory effort — opioid and benzodiazepine overdose cause hypoventilation
Temperature: hyperthermia in serotonin syndrome, hypothermia in opioid/alcohol overdose
preliminary_tests: Carbon monoxide (COHb) if CO poisoning suspected

emergency_medications.name: Naloxone
emergency_medications.dosage: 0.4–2 mg IV/IM/intranasal, repeat q2–3min
emergency_medications.indication: Opioid toxidrome
emergency_medications.warning: Duration shorter than most opioids — infusion may be required. Seizures possible if precipitating acute withdrawal.

emergency_medications.name: Sodium Bicarbonate (IV)
emergency_medications.dosage: 1–2 mEq/kg IV bolus
emergency_medications.indication: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS >120ms or dysrhythmia; salicylate poisoning urinary alkalinisation
emergency_medications.warning: Monitor serum pH (target 7.45–7.55). Hypokalaemia worsens with alkalosis — monitor K+.

age_modifiers.geriatric: Narrower therapeutic windows. Polypharmacy increases drug interaction risk. Accidental overdose common.
age_modifiers.pediatric: Accidental ingestion most common <5y. Intentional overdose in adolescents. Weight-based antidote dosing.
age_modifiers.adult: Establish time of ingestion and agent. Modified-release formulations change kinetics.

domains.label: Geriatric-Specific Presentations
domains.complexity_rationale: Geriatric presentations are frequently atypical with non-specific complaints masking serious underlying pathology. Delirium in elderly is a medical emergency until proven otherwise.
monitoring_criteria: 4AT delirium screen (Alert, Abbreviated Mental Test-4, Attention, Acute onset)
Medication review (polypharmacy adverse effects)
Functional baseline — compare to pre-morbid level
Falls risk: gait, balance, environment
Pressure area assessment
preliminary_tests: Full septic screen (UTI most common delirium cause in elderly)
CT Head if delirium with no clear cause or focal neurological signs

emergency_medications.name: Haloperidol (PO/IM) — low dose
emergency_medications.dosage: 0.5–1 mg PO/IM (geriatric — start low, go slow)
emergency_medications.indication: Acute agitation in hyperactive delirium where patient at risk to self/others
emergency_medications.warning: QT prolongation risk. Avoid in Lewy Body dementia (fatal neuroleptic sensitivity). Not first-line — treat underlying cause first.

age_modifiers.geriatric: All presentations in this domain are geriatric-specific. Apply frailty scoring (CFS). Involve social work early.
age_modifiers.adult: Consider early-onset dementia in adults presenting with cognitive decline <65y.

domains.label: Paediatric-Specific Presentations
domains.complexity_rationale: Paediatric emergencies require age-specific vital sign thresholds and medication dosing. Deterioration can be rapid; compensation masks severity until decompensation.
monitoring_criteria: Paediatric Early Warning Score (PEWS) or TRAP score
Age-appropriate vital sign thresholds (HR, RR, BP all vary by age)
Work of breathing: grunting, nasal flaring, intercostal/subcostal recession
Skin colour and perfusion (mottling, capillary refill >2s)
Hydration: tears, fontanelle (anterior), urine output, skin turgor
preliminary_tests: Blood glucose (point-of-care — hypoglycaemia common in sick children)
Blood culture if fever without source
Lumbar puncture if meningitis suspected (after imaging exclusion of raised ICP)

emergency_medications.name: Dextrose 10% (IV)
emergency_medications.dosage: 5 mL/kg IV bolus (hypoglycaemia in child)
emergency_medications.indication: Hypoglycaemia (BGL <3 mmol/L in child)
emergency_medications.warning: Do not use 50% dextrose in children — causes vein damage. Monitor glucose response at 15 min.

emergency_medications.name: Ceftriaxone (IV)
emergency_medications.dosage: 80–100 mg/kg/day IV (max 4g/day) — meningitis dose
emergency_medications.indication: Suspected bacterial meningitis or meningococcal disease
emergency_medications.warning: Do not delay for LP if clinical concern is high. Add ampicillin if Listeria coverage needed (<3 months). Check allergies.

age_modifiers.pediatric: All presentations in this domain. Use Broselow tape or weight-based calculator for all drug dosing. Involve paediatric specialist early.
age_modifiers.adult: Early-onset conditions (cystic fibrosis, congenital heart disease) may present in young adults.
